final_message:
All three versions are written. Each one passes `s1`, `s2` and `s3` byte-for-byte.

I also made a roughly 228 MB, 2M-line input by repeating `s3` 20 times. All three printed identical output on it. I used three small edge-case files too: an empty file, a file whose last line has no newline, and a file with a blank line plus a query string containing `"`. All three versions agreed on those.

**Algorithm.** Every version does one pass over the file. A line counts as well-formed only if it matches the spec's regex in full; every line counts toward `lines`. For well-formed lines, each version:
- counts the status class from the first status digit;
- turns the path into a template by replacing all-digit segments with `{id}`;
- stores the latency in tenths under that template.

At the end it picks the 10 busiest templates (count descending, then template bytes ascending). It sorts each one's latencies and takes the nearest-rank elements at index `(p*n+99)//100`, using exact integer arithmetic.

**Rust (`rust/src/main.rs`).** On the 2M-line test input it ran in about 0.6 s.
- It reads the whole file and finds line ends with a hand-written 8-bytes-at-a-time newline search.
- It checks each line by hand with no regex, using a path-character lookup table and bounds-checked indexing.
- It builds the template into a reused buffer. The template lookup uses a hash map with a small custom hasher (Fx-style) and allocates only the first time a template appears.
- Latencies sit in one `Vec<u64>` per template, and only the top 10 get sorted.
- I changed `[profile.release]` in `Cargo.toml`: `opt-level=3`, LTO, `codegen-units=1`, `panic=abort`.

**`plain.py`.** On the same input it took about 3.2 s, though timings on this shared machine varied a lot.
- It reads the file in blocks of 256 KB, cut at newlines. Small blocks were clearly faster than 16 MB ones on this machine, probably because they stay in the CPU cache.
- One multiline bytes regex does the whole validation, with `findall` returning only path, status digit and latency.
- Malformed lines are `lines` minus the matches.
- `Counter` counts the status digits.
- A single `re.sub` over the newline-joined paths builds all the templates at once, and one `int` map parses all the latencies.
- A short Python loop appends latencies to per-template lists.

**`fast.py`.** On the same input it took about 3.5 s, so on this run it was slightly slower than `plain.py`, within the machine's noise.
- It uses the same block, regex and bulk-`re.sub` front end, because the variable-length fields make a vectorised parse awkward.
- NumPy handles the rest: `bincount` on the status bytes, a dict-based `np.fromiter` to give each template an integer id, and `np.fromstring` to parse the latencies.
- At the end it works out the counts with `bincount` and extracts and sorts each top template's latencies with a boolean mask.
- It prints through `sys.stdout.buffer`, so the output has `\n` line endings on Windows.

I deleted the scratch files I made for testing.

request.prompt:
You are writing three versions of the same program, one in Rust and two in Python, for a comparison of how
fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Write these three files:

1. `rust/src/main.rs`: Rust, compiled with rustc 1.99 (edition 2024). The Cargo project in `rust/` is set
   up. The only crates you may use are serde (with derive), serde_json, regex and rayon. They are already
   listed in `rust/Cargo.toml` and vendored, so build offline with `cargo build --release --offline` inside
   `rust/`. Do not add other dependencies. You may change the `[profile.release]` settings in
   `rust/Cargo.toml`.
2. `plain.py`: Python 3.13, standard library only.
3. `fast.py`: Python 3.13, standard library plus NumPy 2.2.

Each program is run with the path of one input file as its argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments). It reads that file and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes. The
Python versions are run as `C:\Python313\python.exe plain.py INPUT_PATH` and
`C:\Python313\python.exe fast.py INPUT_PATH`, and the Rust version as the release binary
`rust/target/release/solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Test all three versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside this
folder, and take at most about 45 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time:
never stop a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example
`taskkill /IM python.exe` or `Stop-Process -Name python`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
